questions.prompt: A scaled projected step with symmetric positive definite \(H\) builds the trial point
questions.explanation: The quadratic model \(\nabla f(x)^T (y - x) + \tfrac{1}{2t} (y - x)^T H (y - x)\) is the squared \(H\)-distance from \(y\) to \(x - t H^{-1} \nabla f(x)\), up to a constant. Multiplying by \(H\) instead of \(H^{-1}\) is a different direction. Adding the scaled gradient steps uphill. Minimizing the linear model is a conditional-gradient step, which does not use \(H\).

questions.prompt: Take \(H = \mathrm{diag}(2,\ 4)\), gradient \((8,\ 4)\), step size \(1\), and the current point \((3,\ 4)\). The set is the box \([0,\ 5] \times [0,\ 5]\). What is the second coordinate of the scaled projected step?
questions.explanation: \(H^{-1} \nabla f = (8/2,\ 4/4) = (4,\ 1)\). The trial point is \((3,\ 4) - (4,\ 1) = (-1,\ 3)\). Clipping to the box gives \((0,\ 3)\). The second coordinate is \(3\). Reporting \(-1\) is the unclipped first coordinate. Reporting \(4\) is the old second coordinate. Reporting \(1\) is the scaled gradient's second entry. Because \(H\) is diagonal and the set is a box, each coordinate clips separately.

questions.prompt: Projected Newton is the scaled projected step in which
questions.explanation: The Newton trial point is \(x - \nabla^2 f(x)^{-1} \nabla f(x)\). Projecting that point in the Hessian norm is one scaled projected step with \(t = 1\). The identity scaling is ordinary projected gradient. A positive definite Hessian makes the model convex, but the trial point can still leave the set, so the projection remains. Skipping it would accept an infeasible Newton point.

\(H\) is the identity and the step size is \(1/L\)
the Hessian is ignored and the step is a pure gradient step
the projection is skipped whenever the Hessian is positive definite

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order of one scaled projected iteration on a box, with a diagonal positive definite scaling. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The divisions use the gradient components, so the gradient comes first. The trial point subtracts the scaled vector, so that vector has to exist. Clipping uses the trial point. For a diagonal scaling and a box the \(H\)-norm projection is this coordinatewise clip. Clipping the gradient before the division is a different algorithm.

questions.figure_alt: A two-by-two array with labels on the diagonal.
steps: Evaluate the gradient at the current point.
Divide each component of that gradient by the matching diagonal entry of the scaling, then multiply by the step size.
Subtract the resulting vector from the current point to get the trial point.
Clip each coordinate of that trial point to the box.

questions.prompt: Which of these matrices can be the scaling \(H\) in a scaled projected step?
questions.explanation:
The scaling has to be symmetric positive definite, so the model has a unique minimizer and \(H^{-1}\) exists.
• \(\mathrm{diag}(2,\ 3)\) has positive diagonal entries.
• \(\mathrm{diag}(2,\ 0)\) is singular.
• The matrix with \(2\) on the diagonal and \(1\) off it has eigenvalues \(3\) and \(1\).
• \(\mathrm{diag}(2,\ -1)\) has a negative eigenvalue.
• \(4 I\) is a positive multiple of the identity.
A zero or negative eigenvalue is not a legal scaling.

questions.prompt: With a diagonal scaling, one coordinate has value \(x\), gradient component \(g\), scaling entry \(h\), and step size \(s\). The trial value of that coordinate, before clipping, equals
questions.explanation: The corresponding entry of \(H^{-1} \nabla f\) is \(g/h\). The trial coordinate subtracts \(s\) times that entry from \(x\). Every name appears. Multiplying by \(h\) instead of dividing is the action of \(H\), not of \(H^{-1}\). Dropping \(s\) forces a unit step. Adding \(s g / h\) steps uphill.

questions.prompt: A note runs projected Newton for \(\tfrac32 x^2\) on the interval \([1,\ 4]\), starting at \(2\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The derivative of \(\tfrac32 x^2\) is \(3x\), so the value at \(2\) is \(6\), and the second derivative is \(3\). The Newton point is \(2 - 6/3 = 0\). That point is outside the interval. In one dimension every positive scaling clips to the same place, so the projection of \(0\) onto \([1,\ 4]\) is \(1\). Reporting \(0\) leaves an infeasible point as the answer.

questions.prompt: Using \(H = \mathrm{diag}(4,\ 1)\), project \(z = (8,\ 4)\) onto the half-space \(x_1 + x_2 \le 2\). What is the first coordinate of the projection?
questions.explanation: The excess \(a^T z - 2\) equals \(10\), and \(a^T H^{-1} a = 5/4\), so the multiplier is \(8\). Then \(8 H^{-1} a = (2,\ 8)\), and \((8,\ 4) - (2,\ 8) = (6,\ -4)\). The first coordinate is \(6\). The correction follows \(H^{-1} a\), not the Euclidean normal \((1,\ 1)\). Reporting \(8\) keeps the infeasible first coordinate. Reporting \(2\) is the size of the first correction, not the landing coordinate.

questions.prompt: When \(H\) is diagonal and the set is an axis-aligned box, the scaled projected step
questions.explanation: A diagonal \(H\)-norm separates, and a box separates, so the nearest point clips each coordinate of the trial vector. Off-diagonal entries would couple the coordinates. A positive diagonal is invertible. If a trial coordinate falls outside its interval, clipping moves it to the endpoint. The unclipped Newton point is kept only when it already lies in the box.

is undefined, because a diagonal matrix has no inverse

clips each trial coordinate \(x_i - t g_i / H_{ii}\) to its interval

questions.prompt: If the Newton point lies inside the feasible set, projected Newton
questions.explanation: The projection of a feasible point is itself, in every norm. An interior Newton point is therefore accepted unchanged. Projecting the gradient is a different operation. The step is zero only when the gradient is already zero. The full Hessian, not only its diagonal, defines this trial point.

questions.prompt: For \(2x^2 - 2x\) on the interval \([0,\ 1]\), start at \(2\). The derivative there is \(6\) and the second derivative is \(4\). What is the projected Newton iterate?
questions.explanation: The Newton point is \(2 - 6/4 = 1/2\). The value \(1/2\) lies in \([0,\ 1]\), so the projection leaves it unchanged. Reporting \(2\) skips the step. Reporting \(6/4\) is the length of the Newton step, not the landing point. Reporting \(0\) clips to the wrong end of the interval. Because the Newton point is feasible, projected Newton and unconstrained Newton agree on this step.

questions.prompt: With a fixed positive definite scaling, the usual sublinear guarantee of projected gradient still bounds
questions.explanation: A fixed positive definite scaling changes the inner product in which the projection is taken. The same decrease argument still bounds \(f(x_k) - f^\star\) by a constant over \(k\), for a smooth convex objective and a short enough step. It does not by itself bound a duality gap, and \(\lVert H\rVert\) is data, not a rate. Projected Newton lets \(H\) change with the iterate, which is a different guarantee.

options: \(\lVert H\rVert\), independently of the iterates
the function gap, after the metric is used to define the step
only the angle between successive gradients
the duality gap of a linear program
